chapter_summary:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is a foundational service for the internet and private networks, acting as the phonebook for the digital world. Instead of remembering complex IP addresses like `172.217.160.142`, DNS allows us to use human-readable domain names such as `google.com`. When your RHEL server needs to communicate with another system using its hostname, it queries a DNS server to resolve that hostname into an IP address. Without correctly configured DNS, your server might struggle to access external websites, download updates, or even communicate with other servers in your own data center, leading to frustrating "host not found" errors.

In RHEL, DNS client configuration is typically managed by NetworkManager. When you configure a network connection using `nmcli` or `nmtui` (as covered in the previous chapter), you specify the DNS servers for that connection. NetworkManager then populates the `/etc/resolv.conf` file, which is the primary configuration file for the DNS resolver library. This file lists the IP addresses of DNS servers the system should use, along with a search domain. For example, `nameserver 8.8.8.8` and `nameserver 8.8.4.4` would configure Google's public DNS servers. It's crucial to understand that directly editing `/etc/resolv.conf` is generally discouraged because NetworkManager or other services might overwrite your changes. Instead, modify the DNS settings via NetworkManager for persistence. If you need to temporarily test a different DNS server, you can edit `/etc/resolv.conf`, but be aware that your changes might be lost upon a network restart or reboot.

To troubleshoot DNS resolution, you have powerful command-line tools at your disposal. The `dig` (Domain Information Groper) command is a flexible tool for querying DNS name servers. For instance, `dig google.com` will show you the IP addresses associated with `google.com`, along with detailed information about the query and response. If you want to query a specific DNS server, you can add its IP address: `dig @192.168.1.1 google.com`. The `host` command is a simpler utility for performing DNS lookups. `host google.com` provides a concise output of the IP addresses. If these commands fail or return incorrect information, it indicates a problem with your configured DNS servers or network connectivity to them. A common mistake is using internal DNS servers that are not reachable from the RHEL server, or using external DNS servers when internal hostnames need to be resolved. Always ensure your DNS servers are reachable and can resolve the necessary hostnames.

Beyond DNS, accurate time synchronization is another critical service for any server. Network Time Protocol (NTP) ensures that your system's clock is synchronized with a reliable time source. Why is this so important? Many services, especially those involving security (like Kerberos authentication, SSL/TLS certificates), logging, and distributed applications (databases, clustered file systems), rely heavily on accurate and consistent time across all participating systems. If clocks drift, it can lead to authentication failures, incorrect log timestamps making troubleshooting impossible, data corruption in distributed systems, and certificate validation issues.

In RHEL, the `chronyd` service (provided by the `chrony` package) is the default and recommended NTP client. It's designed to synchronize the system clock more accurately and reliably, even under intermittent network conditions or when the system hibernates. To configure `chronyd`, you primarily edit its configuration file, `/etc/chrony.conf`. Here, you specify the NTP servers (or "pools") your system should synchronize with. A typical configuration might include lines like `pool 2.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst` or `server ntp.example.com iburst`. The `iburst` option sends several queries at once to speed up initial synchronization. After modifying `chrony.conf`, you must restart the `chronyd` service using `sudo systemctl restart chronyd`.

To verify that `chronyd` is working correctly and your system's time is synchronized, you can use the `chronyc` command. `chronyc sources` will list the configured NTP sources and their status, indicating whether they are synchronized (`^` for server, `*` for selected, `+` for candidate). `chronyc tracking` provides detailed information about the synchronization, including the reference ID, stratum, and system offset. A common mistake is forgetting to open the NTP port (UDP 123) in `firewalld` if the server is behind a firewall and needs to reach external NTP sources. Always ensure `firewall-cmd --add-service=ntp` is active if necessary. If `chronyd` reports no sources or is not synchronized, check network connectivity to the NTP servers and your `firewalld` configuration.

screens.title: Configuring DNS and NTP Services
screens.subtitle: Make name resolution and time reliable on your RHEL systems

narration.text: In this lesson we'll make two foundational services reliable on a RHEL server: DNS name resolution and system time via NTP. DNS translates human names like google. com into IP addresses your server can use. When DNS is misconfigured, you can ping 8.8.8.8 but still see 'host not found' errors. We'll show how NetworkManager provides DNS settings to /etc/resolv. conf, and when to change connection profiles instead of editing that file directly. Next, we'll cover time synchronization: why accurate system time matters for authentication, certificates, logs, and distributed systems, and how chronyd is the recommended NTP client on RHEL. You'll see how /etc/chrony. conf lists pools or servers and how the iburst option speeds initial sync. Finally, we'll practice key commands: nmcli to set DNS, dig and host to query DNS servers, and chronyc to inspect NTP sources and tracking. By the end, you'll be able to configure persistent DNS, diagnose resolution problems with dig and host, install and configure chronyd, and verify that your system clock is synchronized. Think about services in your environment that would break if names or time were wrong.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Correct DNS and synchronized time prevent connectivity errors, authentication failures, and logging confusion. These are prerequisites for a healthy RHEL server.

screens.title: What is DNS and the resolver?
screens.subtitle: How name-to-IP resolution works and why it matters

narration.text: DNS is the system that maps human-readable domain names to IP addresses. On your RHEL server a resolver component performs this mapping by asking configured DNS servers for the address of a hostname. Think of the resolver as your server's phonebook: you ask for a name and it returns a number. For example, resolving google. com yields addresses like 172.217.160.142; the server does not need to memorize that. This matters because nearly every network operation that uses hostnames depends on it — package managers, remote login, monitoring agents, and inter-service communication will fail if names cannot be resolved. A common misconception is to assume that DNS only affects external websites; internal hostnames used within a data center are equally dependent on proper DNS. Another misunderstanding is to edit /etc/resolv. conf directly for persistent changes; on RHEL NetworkManager populates that file from connection profiles and will overwrite manual edits. In practice you configure DNS in the network connection so settings survive reboots. Example: setting a connection's ipv4. dns to 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4 ensures your resolver can query Google's servers. Key takeaway: DNS resolution is a fundamental client-side step every service relies on; if it breaks, many higher-level features fail in ways that look unrelated to networking.

keyIdea.title: DNS is foundational
keyIdea.text: If the resolver can't turn names into IPs, many services will fail even when basic IP connectivity works.

content.html:
Core Concept

What the resolver does

The resolver queries DNS servers to translate hostnames into IP addresses so applications can open connections using numeric addresses.

Analogy: phonebook
Ask for a name, receive a number. The resolver asks DNS servers and returns addresses to clients.
Common misconceptions
  • Editing /etc/resolv.conf directly makes persistent changes — not reliable with NetworkManager.
  • DNS only affects external sites — internal hostnames also require DNS.
Key Takeaway
Resolver failures manifest as 'host not found' even when raw IP connectivity works. Fixing DNS fixes many downstream errors.
Concrete example
# Example resolver query
$ dig google.com
; <<>> DiG 9.11.3-1 <<>> google.com
;; ANSWER SECTION:
google.com. 299 IN A 172.217.160.142
Why it matters in practice
If a package update or a remote host lookup fails because names cannot be resolved, you'll see errors unrelated to the application's logic. Correct resolver settings restore normal operations.

screens.title: How DNS queries flow from client to server
screens.subtitle: Steps a resolver takes and how to target a specific DNS server

narration.text: A DNS query follows a simple flow on your server. First, an application asks the resolver library to look up a hostname. The resolver consults the system's configuration — typically /etc/resolv. conf — to find one or more nameserver addresses. It sends a UDP query to a nameserver; if the primary does not respond, it retries another server listed. The nameserver may return an answer from cache, or it may perform recursion, asking upstream servers until it finds the authoritative response. Practically, you rarely control the chain of recursive queries, but you can target a particular DNS server for testing. For example, dig @192.168.1.1 google. com runs the same query but forces that server to answer. That helps distinguish whether a general resolution failure is due to unreachable DNS servers or incorrect DNS zone data. A common pitfall is using an external public resolver when you need to resolve private internal hostnames; always ensure the configured servers can resolve the names you rely on. When troubleshooting, check reachability to each listed nameserver and use targeted queries to isolate where answers are failing.

keyIdea.title: Query targeting
keyIdea.text: Use targeted queries like dig @server name to determine whether resolution fails because of server reachability or incorrect DNS data.

content.html:
Process Flow

DNS query lifecycle

Step 1 — Application request
A process asks the resolver to look up a hostname.
Step 2 — Resolver consults /etc/resolv.conf
It reads nameserver entries and chooses one to query.
Step 3 — UDP query and response
The resolver sends a UDP query. The server returns an answer or forwards the request.
Example targeted query
dig @192.168.1.1 google.com
; <<>> DiG <<>> @192.168.1.1 google.com
;; ANSWER SECTION:
google.com. 299 IN A 172.217.160.142
Troubleshooting tip
If dig to a listed server times out, check network reachability to that nameserver before changing DNS entries.
Key Takeaway
Targeted queries isolate whether the problem is the server or the data; verify each listed nameserver is reachable.

screens.title: NetworkManager and /etc/resolv.conf
screens.subtitle: How RHEL manages DNS client settings and persistence

narration.text: On RHEL the DNS client configuration is usually managed by NetworkManager. When you edit a connection profile using nmcli or nmtui, NetworkManager writes the configured DNS server addresses into the resolver configuration used by applications. That main file is /etc/resolv. conf. It lists nameserver lines and optional search domains. A common mistake is directly editing /etc/resolv. conf and expecting changes to persist across network restarts; NetworkManager will often overwrite manual edits with the connection's configured values. For temporary tests it's acceptable to edit /etc/resolv. conf, but for lasting changes you must modify the network connection through NetworkManager. For example, sudo nmcli connection modify my-static-eth0 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4" updates the profile, and sudo nmcli connection up my-static-eth0 reapplies the settings. Also be mindful of DHCP: if your interface uses DHCP, the DHCP server may supply DNS servers. If persistent custom DNS is required, set it on the connection or adjust DHCP server settings. The practical rule is: make DNS changes via NetworkManager profiles, then verify /etc/resolv. conf reflects them. NetworkManager and /etc/resolv.conf means modify connection profiles so changes survive reboots; /etc/resolv.conf is a runtime reflection of those profiles.. In practical terms, how rhel manages dns client settings and persistence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Make DNS changes in NetworkManager
keyIdea.text: Modify connection profiles so changes survive reboots; /etc/resolv.conf is a runtime reflection of those profiles.

content.html:
Definition

NetworkManager drives resolv.conf

NetworkManager populates /etc/resolv.conf from connection profiles. Edit the connection, not resolv.conf, for persistence.

Example nmcli changes
sudo nmcli connection modify my-static-eth0 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"
sudo nmcli connection up my-static-eth0
Misconception to avoid
Manually editing /etc/resolv.conf makes permanent changes — NetworkManager or DHCP may overwrite them.
Typical /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by NetworkManager
search example.com
nameserver 8.8.8.8
nameserver 8.8.4.4
Key Takeaway
For stable DNS configuration, set DNS on the NetworkManager connection profile and reactivate the connection to apply changes.

screens.title: Practical nmcli and resolv.conf verification
screens.subtitle: Commands to set DNS and verify system behavior

narration.text: Let's walk through the exact commands you will use to configure and verify DNS. Start by modifying the connection profile with nmcli. For a connection named my-static-eth0 use sudo nmcli connection modify my-static-eth0 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4" then run sudo nmcli connection up my-static-eth0 to reactivate the profile and apply the settings immediately. After applying changes, check /etc/resolv. conf with cat /etc/resolv. conf to confirm nameserver entries were populated. If your interface is named differently, substitute its connection name; in the assessment the example uses System enp0s3. A common troubleshooting practice is to temporarily edit /etc/resolv. conf to test a different server, but remember such edits may be overwritten on network restart. If dig or host returns incorrect information after the change, test dig @server domain to target each nameserver directly and identify reachability problems. Always validate both that the resolver file contains the right IPs and that queries to those servers succeed. This pairing of configuration and verification prevents wasted troubleshooting time later. Practical nmcli and resolv.conf verification means every nmcli change should be followed by checking /etc/resolv.conf and running a targeted dig to confirm the resolvers answer as expected.. In practical terms, commands to set dns and verify system behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Change, then verify
keyIdea.text: Every nmcli change should be followed by checking /etc/resolv.conf and running a targeted dig to confirm the resolvers answer as expected.

content.html:
Hands-on

Set DNS and verify

Set DNS on the connection
sudo nmcli connection modify my-static-eth0 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"
sudo nmcli connection up my-static-eth0
Check resolver file
cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by NetworkManager
nameserver 8.8.8.8
nameserver 8.8.4.4
Test each server
dig @192.168.1.1 google.com
If it times out, address reachability first before changing DNS entries.
Temporary tests
Editing /etc/resolv.conf is useful for short tests, but changes may not persist on restart.
Key Takeaway

Make the change in NetworkManager, reactivate the connection, and then test with dig or host to confirm resolution works.

screens.title: Using dig for flexible DNS queries
screens.subtitle: Inspect responses and target specific servers when troubleshooting

narration.text: dig is a flexible diagnostic tool for DNS. A plain dig domain query returns answer sections with the resolved IP addresses and metadata about the query and response. For targeted testing, prefix the query with an at-sign and a server address, for example dig @192.168.1.1 google. com. This forces the resolver to ask that server and is the fastest way to determine whether the server or the network path to it is the issue. dig output contains several sections: the question, answer, authority, and additional sections. Look in the answer section for IP addresses and in the status line for errors. If you see a SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, or no answer, the problem may be with the authoritative server or with recursion policies on the nameserver. dig also helps when testing name resolution changes: after modifying your connection, run dig to confirm the resolvers you set return correct answers. Remember dig is verbose; when you want a concise response for quick checks, use host, which we'll cover next. A common misread is to assume that a cached answer is necessarily current; if zones were just updated, querying a specific authoritative server may be needed to see the new data.

keyIdea.title: dig for deep inspection
keyIdea.text: Use dig's detailed output to see answers, authority, and status; target servers to isolate where responses are generated.

content.html:
Tooling

dig: deep DNS inspection

Verbose query
dig google.com
; <<>> DiG <<>> google.com
;; ANSWER SECTION:
google.com. 299 IN A 172.217.160.142
;; Query time: 30 msec
Target a specific server
dig @192.168.1.1 google.com
Use this to verify whether a configured nameserver answers correctly.
Interpreting results
  • Answer section: contains resolved addresses.
  • Status lines may show SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, or successful codes.
Key Takeaway

dig is the go-to tool when you need full details about DNS responses and to test specific servers directly.

screens.title: dig vs host
screens.subtitle: When to use verbose output or a concise lookup

narration.text: dig and host are complementary command-line DNS utilities. dig provides detailed debugging information: the question, answer, authority, and additional sections, plus timings and flags. Use dig when you need to inspect the full response, check status codes, or query a specific server with the at-sign notation. host, in contrast, is simpler and produces concise results listing the IPs for a name. host is useful for quick checks in scripts or when you want a readable one-line result. An example: running host redhat. com returns a short list of addresses, while dig redhat. com yields detailed sections and additional metadata. A common misconception is to assume either tool can fix DNS; both are read-only diagnostics. Choose dig when diagnosing complex failures or testing a particular nameserver; choose host when you need a fast, human-friendly confirmation that a name resolves. Practically, use both: start with host for a quick pass, and escalate to dig when problems persist or you need authoritative information. dig vs host means start with host for quick checks; use dig for deeper debugging and targeted server queries.. In practical terms, when to use verbose output or a concise lookup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use the right tool
keyIdea.text: Start with host for quick checks; use dig for deeper debugging and targeted server queries.

content.html:
Comparison

dig vs host

host example
host redhat.com
redhat.com has address 104.129.202.49
dig example (brief)
dig redhat.com
;; ANSWER SECTION:
redhat.com. 299 IN A 104.129.202.49
Practical choice
Use host for quick confirmation, dig for debugging and server-specific queries.
Key Takeaway
Both tools are read-only diagnostics. Use the concise tool first, and escalate to detail when needed.
Misconception
Neither tool changes DNS. They only reveal what the configured servers return.

screens.title: Common DNS troubleshooting steps
screens.subtitle: A disciplined checklist when name resolution fails

narration.text: When a server cannot resolve names but can reach IP addresses, follow a checklist to isolate the fault. First, confirm /etc/resolv. conf contains nameserver entries; if it's empty, NetworkManager connection profiles may lack DNS settings. Next, run ping against a DNS server IP to check network reachability. Then use dig @server domain for each nameserver listed to ensure the server answers queries. If queries fail, confirm firewall rules allow DNS traffic and that the nameserver itself is reachable from your network. Another frequent cause is using external public servers while internal hostnames must be resolved by internal DNS; if internal names are needed, configure the internal nameserver. If using DHCP, verify the DHCP server supplies the correct DNS and that NetworkManager applies it. Finally, when changes are applied, test resolution again with dig and host to confirm fixes. Document each step and the outcome; that record helps you and others reproduce or undo changes if needed. The disciplined approach minimizes guesswork and avoids unnecessary configuration churn. Common DNS troubleshooting steps means check resolv.conf, test reachability, query each server directly, verify firewall and dhcp roles, and then re-test resolution.. In practical terms, a disciplined checklist when name resolution fails. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Follow a checklist
keyIdea.text: Check resolv.conf, test reachability, query each server directly, verify firewall and DHCP roles, and then re-test resolution.

content.html:
Troubleshooting

Checklist for resolution failures

1. Inspect resolver file
cat /etc/resolv.conf — ensure nameserver entries exist.
2. Network reachability
ping the DNS server IP to confirm it's reachable.
3. Targeted queries
dig @192.168.1.1 example.com — test each server directly.
4. Firewall
Ensure firewalld allows DNS traffic if filtering is in place.
5. DHCP vs static
If using DHCP, confirm the server provides correct DNS; otherwise set static DNS in the connection.
Key Takeaway

Work methodically from configuration to network to server to avoid changing the wrong component.

screens.title: Why accurate time matters (NTP)
screens.subtitle: Effects of clock drift on authentication, certificates, and logs

narration.text: Accurate time is essential on servers because many subsystems and protocols rely on consistent clocks. Authentication systems such as Kerberos require clocks to be closely aligned; skewed clocks can cause authentication failures. SSL/TLS certificate validation depends on the local system time to determine validity windows; incorrect time can make valid certificates appear expired or not yet valid. Logging and incident correlation across multiple hosts require synchronized timestamps; without synchronization, tracing events through distributed systems becomes unreliable. Databases and clustered filesystems may also depend on time ordering; large drifts can cause confusion or even data integrity issues. Network Time Protocol, or NTP, provides a standard way to synchronize clocks across networks. On RHEL the recommended client is chronyd, which handles intermittent networks and hibernation better than older clients. Configure chronyd with pools or servers in /etc/chrony. conf, enable the chronyd service, and verify synchronization. Treat time like a first-class service: if it is wrong, many unrelated problems will surface and be harder to debug. Why accurate time matters (NTP) means clock drift can break authentication, invalidate certificates, and ruin log correlation; keep servers synchronized with ntp.. In practical terms, effects of clock drift on authentication, certificates, and logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Time affects many systems
keyIdea.text: Clock drift can break authentication, invalidate certificates, and ruin log correlation; keep servers synchronized with NTP.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why NTP matters

Authentication, certificate validation, logging, and distributed systems depend on accurate and consistent clocks across hosts.

Concrete example
If clocks drift, Kerberos tickets may be rejected and SSL certificates may appear invalid.
Misconception
Manually setting the clock is a temporary fix. A synchronized NTP client maintains alignment automatically.
Recommended client on RHEL
chronyd — configured via /etc/chrony.conf and controlled with systemctl.
Key Takeaway

Treat time as foundational. Use chronyd to keep clocks aligned so security and logging work reliably.

screens.title: Configure chronyd and verify with chronyc
screens.subtitle: Edit /etc/chrony.conf, start chronyd, and interpret chronyc output

narration.text: To configure chronyd start by installing the chrony package if it is not present. Then edit /etc/chrony. conf to specify servers or pools. The chapter suggests using pool 0. rhel. pool. ntp. org iburst through pool 3. rhel. pool. ntp. org iburst. The iburst option sends several packets at startup to accelerate initial synchronization. You may also add allow lines to permit local network clients if you plan to serve NTP. After editing the config, enable and start chronyd with sudo systemctl enable --now chronyd, and check its status with sudo systemctl status chronyd. To monitor synchronization, use chronyc sources -v which lists configured sources with symbols indicating their state: one symbol marks the selected or preferred source. chronyc tracking provides the reference ID, stratum, and system time offset; a small system offset means clocks are in agreement. If chronyd reports sources as unreachable, a common cause is firewalld blocking UDP 123 — add the ntp service via firewall-cmd and reload. Always wait a few minutes after starting chronyd for synchronization to stabilize before taking action based on the system clock.

keyIdea.title: Configure, start, verify
keyIdea.text: Add pool lines with iburst, enable chronyd, and use chronyc sources and tracking to confirm a small system offset and a selected source.

content.html:
Practice

chronyd configuration and verification

Suggested /etc/chrony.conf entries
# Use public NTP servers from the pool project.
pool 0.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst
pool 1.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts so you can recall them quickly. First, the DNS resolver is the client-side component that queries nameservers to turn hostnames into IP addresses; it is critical for almost all networked services. Second, /etc/resolv. conf lists nameserver addresses and search domains, but on RHEL NetworkManager typically generates and manages this file from connection profiles. Third, dig is a diagnostic Swiss army knife that shows detailed DNS responses and can target a specific server when you prefix with at-sign notation. Keep these three concepts in mind when you configure and debug name resolution. Each is a practical checkpoint: ensure resolv. conf reflects your intended nameservers, use dig to inspect answers and status codes, and remember that NetworkManager is the source of truth for persistent DNS on RHEL. These ideas will help you resolve many common name-resolution problems efficiently.

keyIdea.text: Resolver behavior, the role of /etc/resolv.conf, and using dig are the fastest routes to diagnose DNS issues.

narration.text: A second short summary covers NTP and verification tools. chronyd is the recommended NTP client on RHEL; configure it via /etc/chrony. conf using pool or server entries, and include iburst to speed initial synchronization. Start and enable chronyd with systemctl enable --now chronyd. Use chronyc sources to inspect configured NTP sources and chronyc tracking to read system offset and reference. When sources are shown as unreachable, check firewalld because UDP port 123 blocking is a frequent cause. Finally, pair configuration edits with verification commands: after configuring DNS or chronyd, run the appropriate commands to confirm the service functions. This minimizes downtime and stops transient changes from becoming permanent problems. Carry these verification habits into your daily operations: configure, start, then verify.
